A profitable sale can need cash first: follow inventory, supplier terms and customer receipts

Use a fixed-year batch-trading ledger to separate simplified profit from cash, calculate an initial funding need and reconcile the trade balances between them.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow repeated inventory batches through a fixed 365-day cash window

Interactive planning lab

Minimum starting cash for a non-negative day-end ledger$11,180
Extra initial cash above the entered business balance$1,180
Simplified 365-day operating result before owner withdrawals$10,700

Original deterministic batch-trading illustration over days 0–365. Identical batches are ordered at the chosen spacing, beginning on day zero; each is sold in full after the entered stock days, collected in full after the buyer delay, and paid to the supplier after the supplier delay measured from the order. Supplier credit and customer terms are assumptions, not accepted offers or permitted late payments. Every supported batch is sold, collected and paid within day 365. Inventory is recorded at batch cost; customer invoices at the entered sale price. Simplified profit recognises batch revenue less batch inventory cost on sale day, and the cash overhead on each day 1–365. Overhead continues through the full fixed year even after the final batch settles. Net trading cash records actual collections less supplier payments and the same overhead; starting cash is added only to the separate cash-balance view. Daily netting omits intraday funding needs. Negative cash balances are unfunded positions, not automatic credit. No tax, interest, fees, discounts, wages beyond entered costs, owner withdrawal, unsold stock, bad debt or depreciation is modeled. The displayed per-batch interval uses authored event lags, not average-day ratios estimated from actual financial statements.

The central idea

Profit, a cash-conversion interval and the cash needed to survive the calendar are different measures. Prepare the business funding path before relying on its income for household spending.

01

Draw the order, supplier payment, sale and customer receipt separately

A small business can sell at a positive margin while its owner still needs cash to fund the period before the customer pays. The selling price alone does not tell you whether stock purchases, supplier bills and operating costs can be paid on their actual dates.

The example orders six identical batches, beginning on day zero and then every thirty days. Each batch costs CAD 5,000 and is sold in full for CAD 8,000 thirty days after ordering. The supplier is paid fifteen days after the order, while the customer pays thirty days after the sale.

For the first batch, the dates are therefore order on day zero, supplier payment on day fifteen, sale on day thirty and customer collection on day sixty. These are original assumed terms and guaranteed modeled receipts, not supplier quotes, observed collection averages or an assessment of a real customer.

02

The payment-to-collection interval is measured in days, not dollars

BDC’s cash-conversion-cycle guide relates inventory, receivables and payables timing when explaining business cash flow. Its financial-statement approach uses average days calculated from balances and turnover. This website instead supplies explicit fixed event lags for identical batches.

Under those lags, each supplier payment precedes its customer collection by 30 + 30 − 15 = 45 days. The first waterfall reconciles that authored interval. It is not an estimated industry cash-conversion ratio, a likelihood of payment or a required cash amount.

Forty-five days on its own does not determine the funding need. Batch size, order spacing, sale margin, overhead and available starting cash matter too. Changing the amount purchased can change the cash requirement while leaving all three timing assumptions unchanged.

03

Recognise the sale margin separately from when cash moves

The model recognises a batch’s CAD 8,000 revenue less its CAD 5,000 inventory cost on the sale day. That produces a CAD 3,000 margin for each of the six full sales, or CAD 18,000 before the separately entered overhead.

Cash operating overhead is CAD 20 on each of days one through 365, totalling CAD 7,300. It continues through the fixed full-year window, including after the last batch settles. The resulting simplified annual operating result is CAD 10,700, before owner withdrawals and the other excluded items.

Net trading cash uses different dates: it records actual customer collections, supplier payments and the same daily overhead. Starting cash is excluded from that measure so it does not look like sales revenue or profit. The profit and net-trading-cash lines can differ during the year even though all modeled customers eventually pay.

04

A positive annual result does not fund the earlier trough

The business starts with CAD 10,000. Before the first customer receipt on day sixty, two CAD 5,000 supplier payments have already left on days fifteen and forty-five. By the end of day fifty-nine, another CAD 1,180 of overhead has been paid.

The cash ledger at that point is CAD 10,000 − CAD 10,000 − CAD 1,180 = minus CAD 1,180. The model therefore needs at least CAD 11,180 of starting cash to keep every day-end non-negative, which is CAD 1,180 more than the entered amount.

Without that additional funding, the negative ledger is an unfunded position. It is not an authorised overdraft or evidence that a bank would lend the amount. Later customer receipts do not retroactively fund the day-fifty-nine payments.

At day 365, after all six sales have been collected and all suppliers paid, the original cash plus net trading cash is CAD 20,700. That positive endpoint does not remove the earlier trough. This is why a household cannot rely on an annual business profit figure alone when planning withdrawals for personal bills.

05

Explain the difference using stock, invoices and supplier amounts due

The selected snapshot is day forty. The second batch has been ordered but not sold, so unsold inventory is recorded at CAD 5,000 of batch cost. The first sale has created an unpaid CAD 8,000 customer invoice. The second supplier payment is not yet due, leaving CAD 5,000 payable.

The reconciliation is CAD 5,000 inventory + CAD 8,000 receivable − CAD 5,000 payable = CAD 8,000. At the same day-end, the simplified operating result is CAD 2,200 while net trading cash is minus CAD 5,800, also a difference of CAD 8,000.

The final waterfall shows that identity for the selected day. It does not value stock at an assumed liquidation price or establish that an unpaid invoice can be collected immediately. It is a reconciliation of the modeled trade balances, excluding starting cash and the rest of a real business balance sheet.

Once all batches, customer invoices and supplier amounts have cleared, the difference becomes zero. Both cumulative measures then end at CAD 10,700 after the fixed year’s overhead.

06

Change agreed payment terms without confusing them with margins

The matrix changes the customer delay after a sale and the supplier-payment delay after an order. Each cell recomputes the extra starting cash needed over the same 365-day period, holding the batch prices, order spacing, stock days, overhead and entered starting cash fixed.

Within this particular model, changing only those payment lags does not change the annual operating result because every batch is sold, collected and paid before year-end. It does change when the money is available and when supplier cash is required.

A customer receipt can precede its supplier payment when the assumed supplier term is sufficiently long. The per-batch interval then becomes negative. That does not erase the payable or make the temporarily high cash balance safe to distribute without considering later obligations.

The alternative terms are assumed to be agreed. Delaying a supplier beyond a real due date is not the same thing as negotiating a longer term, and any discount, penalty, financing charge or change in price would need its own cash flow.

07

Keep business funding and household spending on connected but separate plans

  1. Map inventory orders, full sales, collection dates and supplier due dates.
  2. Include operating costs through the full reporting period.
  3. Find the largest day-end funding gap before planning withdrawals.
  4. Review invoices, stock and unpaid suppliers when profit differs from cash.
  5. Add taxes, financing and owner spending explicitly before deciding what is available personally.

The charts assume full sales and collections at the entered values, with no bad debt, unsold stock, discounts, interest, fees, depreciation or tax. Daily cash is netted at the end of each day; earlier intraday payment deadlines can require more liquidity. No owner withdrawals are included.

The operating result is a deliberately simplified teaching measure. It does not represent a formal financial statement or determine taxable income. A useful personal plan needs a separate, dated decision about what the business can release after its own obligations are funded.
